description_ru: Классическая физика утверждает, что Солнце не должно гореть. Квантовое туннелирование объясняет, как протоны всё же сливаются и почему звезда светит миллиарды лет.
text:
By every classical calculation, the Sun should not shine. At its centre, the temperature is about fifteen million kelvin, which sounds extreme, yet it is not nearly extreme enough. The reason is that the Sun is powered by the fusion of hydrogen nuclei, which are single protons, and protons carry positive electric charge. Two of them repel each other with a force that grows ferociously as they approach, and to bring them close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them together, a proton would need to be moving astonishingly fast, which means a temperature of roughly ten billion degrees. The Sun's core falls short by a factor of several hundred.

For decades this was an embarrassment. By the 1920s astronomers such as Arthur Eddington had argued that nuclear reactions must be the Sun's energy source, and Eddington famously told a sceptic that he was welcome to go and find a hotter place. But the sums did not add up. The solution came from an unexpected direction, namely the quantum theory that physicists had been developing to understand atoms.

In quantum mechanics, a particle is not a tiny billiard ball with a definite location. It is described by a wave function, which spreads over a region of space and gives the probability of finding the particle at any given spot. When such a wave meets a barrier, it does not stop abruptly. Its amplitude decays rapidly inside the barrier, but if the barrier is thin enough, a small remainder emerges on the other side. That means there is a real, though usually tiny, probability that the particle will appear beyond the wall without ever having had the energy to climb over it. This is called quantum tunnelling.

It is worth pausing on how strange this is. Tunnelling is not a trick of clever engineering; it is a direct consequence of the same equations that explain the colours of atoms, the stability of matter and the working of every transistor in your phone. The idea was first applied to the nucleus in 1928 by the Russian-born physicist George Gamow, who used it to explain why certain radioactive atoms emit alpha particles. The following year Robert Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans realised that the same effect could allow protons in stars to fuse at temperatures far below the classical requirement. Later, Hans Bethe worked out the detailed sequence of reactions, work for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1967.

The numbers are humbling. Any individual proton in the Sun's core collides with others billions of times each second, yet the chance that a given collision results in fusion is vanishingly small. A typical proton waits, on average, for something like ten billion years before it finally succeeds, which is roughly the whole lifetime of the Sun. The star shines not because fusion is likely for any one proton, but because the core contains such an immense number of them, around ten to the power of fifty-seven, that a colossal quantity of fusions occurs every second.

The principal chain of reactions, known as the proton-proton chain, is also slow for another reason. The first step requires one proton to turn into a neutron, forming a deuterium nucleus, and that depends on the weak nuclear force, which is truly feeble. This bottleneck acts as a natural governor. If the first step were easy, the Sun would burn through its hydrogen in a flash. Instead, it releases energy at a gentle and astonishingly steady rate, about as much per cubic metre as a compost heap, and has done so for nearly five billion years.

Each second, the Sun fuses roughly six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and in doing so converts about four million tonnes of matter into energy, in accordance with Einstein's famous equation. The energy emerges first as gamma rays, but these are absorbed and re-emitted countless times on their journey outwards, a random walk that takes tens of thousands of years or more before light finally reaches the surface. By contrast, the ghostly neutrinos produced in the same reactions fly straight out of the Sun and reach Earth in about eight minutes. Detecting them was one of the great triumphs of experimental physics, and the first measurements, made deep underground in the late 1960s, confirmed that the Sun really does run on fusion. They also found only about a third of the expected number, a puzzle that took three more decades to solve, when physicists showed that neutrinos change their identity on the way, a phenomenon called oscillation.

Not every star follows the same recipe. In stars appreciably heavier than the Sun, whose cores are hotter, a different sequence called the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle dominates, using those heavier nuclei as catalysts. It is far more sensitive to temperature, so such stars burn their fuel furiously and live for a few hundred million years at most, and the heaviest for only a few million, a blink compared with the Sun's ten billion. Even in our own star it contributes about one per cent of the output, a quiet reminder that the universe runs several engines at once.

So the sunlight on your face owes its existence to a strange loophole in the laws of the very small. The Sun is, in a sense, a machine for exploiting improbability on a staggering scale. Without quantum mechanics, the sky would be dark, and nobody would be around to wonder why.

questions.question: Why does classical physics say the Sun should not shine?
questions.answer: Protons repel each other, so fusion would need billions of degrees, far hotter than the Sun's core.

questions.question: What is quantum tunnelling?
questions.answer: A particle can appear on the far side of a barrier it does not have the energy to climb.
